Description: explicit — route shields missing badge on the open OpenMapTiles stack
prompt: I'm using an open OpenMapTiles / OSM-based vector basemap with MapLibre GL JS (no Mapbox account). My interstate and US highway shields render as bare floating numbers with no shield badge behind them; the numbers are fine. My tiles do populate network, ref, and ref_length. Which exact sprite image names do the shield layers expect, and how do I get the badges to appear without editing the layers?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  

The shield layers that come with the **OpenMapTiles** (or any MapLibre‑GL style that was copied from Mapbox‑Streets) look for **exactly the following sprite‑image keys**:

| Shield type | Sprite name (key) |
|-------------|-------------------|
| Generic numeric shields (1 – 20) | `road-shield-1`, `road-shield-2`, `road-shield-3`, … `road-shield-20` |
| US Interstate (red “I‑xx”) | `road-shield-us-interstate` |
| US Highway (black “US xx”) | `road-shield-us-us` |
| US Highway alternate / business (white “US xx‑A”) | `road-shield-us-us-2` |

If those four‑digit keys are present in the **sprite sheet** (the `*.png` + `*.json` pair that you point to with the `sprite` property of the style), the numbers you already see in the `ref`/`ref_length` fields will automatically be drawn on top of the correct badge.

---

## Why the badges disappear

When you use the OpenMapTiles vector tiles **without** the accompanying sprite sheet, the style still creates the text‑symbol layers (`road-number-*`) but it can’t find any image to use as a background. The result is exactly what you described: floating numbers with no badge.

The fix is **only** to supply a sprite sheet that contains the keys above – you do **not** have to touch the style JSON at all.

---

## How to get a working sprite sheet (no layer editing required)

### 1. Grab the official OpenMapTiles sprite

The OpenMapTiles repository already ships a ready‑made sprite that contains every shield the style expects.

```text
https://github.com/openmaptiles/openmaptiles/tree/master/styles/positron/sprite
```

Download the two files:

* `sprite@2x.png` (high‑DPI version) – **or** `sprite.png` for normal DPI  
* `sprite@2x.json` (or `sprite.json`)

Place them on a web‑accessible location (e.g. your own CDN, GitHub Pages, or the same server that serves the style JSON) and point the style at them:

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sprite": "https://my.cdn.com/omt-sprite/sprite",
  ...
}
```

> **Note:** The URL must **not** include the file extension; MapLibre will automatically request `sprite.json` and `sprite.png` (or the `@2x` versions when the device pixel ratio > 1).

### 2. If you want a custom colour/size – generate your own

If you prefer a different colour palette or need extra shields (e.g. state‑level shields), you can generate a sprite yourself:

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **openmaptiles/shields** (GitHub) | Contains the SVG source for every US shield (interstate, US‑highway, US‑alternate) plus a tiny Node script (`generate-sprite.js`) that rasterises the SVGs into a Mapbox‑compatible sprite (`png + json`). |
| **mapbox‑shield‑generator** (npm) | A more generic generator that can take any SVG set and output a sprite. |
| **SpriteZero** (online) | Drag‑and‑drop PNGs + names and it builds the JSON for you. |

Typical workflow with the official repo:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openmaptiles/shields.git
cd shields
npm install   # installs sharp, mapbox‑sprite, etc.
node generate-sprite.js   # creates sprite.png + sprite.json
```

The script already names the images exactly as the style expects (`road-shield-us-interstate`, `road-shield-us-us`, `road‑shield‑us‑us‑2`, plus `road‑shield‑1` … `road‑shield‑20`). Just copy the resulting files to your server and reference them as shown above.

### 3. Verify the sprite contains the required keys

Open the generated `sprite.json` in a text editor or in the browser (`https://my.cdn.com/omt-sprite/sprite.json`). You should see entries like:

```json
{
  "road-shield-1": {"width":30,"height":30,"x":0,"y":0,"pixelRatio":2},
  "road-shield-2": {"width":30,"height":30,"x":30,"y":0,"pixelRatio":2},
  ...
  "road-shield-us-interstate": {"width":30,"height":30,"x":600,"y":0,"pixelRatio":2},
  "road-shield-us-us": {"width":30,"height":30,"x":630,"y":0,"pixelRatio":2},
  "road-shield-us-us-2": {"width":30,"height":30,"x":660,"y":0,"pixelRatio":2}
}
```

If those keys are present, the style will automatically pick the right badge for each feature based on the `network` and `ref` properties that you already have in the tiles.

---

## Quick checklist – get shields working in < 5 minutes

1. **Download** the official sprite (`sprite.png` + `sprite.json`) from the OpenMapTiles repo (or generate your own).  
2. **Host** the two files on a URL that is reachable from the page that loads the map.  
3. **Edit the style JSON** (once) to point to that URL:

   ```json
   "sprite": "https://my.cdn.com/omt-sprite/sprite"
   ```

4. **Reload** the page. The numbers should now appear on top of the proper shield background (interstate red, US black, generic gray, etc.).

That’s it – no need to touch any of the `road-number-*` layers, `filter`s, or `icon-image` expressions. The style does all the work; it just needs the sprite sheet that contains the exact image names listed above. Happy mapping!

If those images are missing from the sprite sheet that your MapLibre GL JS map is using, the style can still read the `ref`/`network` values (so you see the numbers) but it has nothing to draw **behind** the numbers – you get “floating digits”.

All you have to do is point the style at a sprite sheet that contains those 12 images (or add them yourself). No layer‑style changes are required.

Below is a short guide that tells you:

1. **What each sprite name represents** (so you know which badge you’re getting).

## 1. What the 12 sprite names mean

| Sprite name | Typical badge that appears | Network values that map to it (as used by the default style) |
|-------------|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `road-shield-1` | **US Interstate** (red‑white‑red) | `US:I` (e.g. `I‑5`, `I‑95`) |
| `road-shield-2` | **US U.S. Highway** (black‑white) | `US:US` (e.g. `US‑20`, `US‑101`) |
| `road-shield-3` | **US State Highway** (blue‑white) | `US:AL`, `US:CA`, … (any `US:<state‑abbr>`) |
| `road-shield-4` | **US County Road** (green‑white) | `US:CO`, `US:TX`, … (any `US:<state‑abbr>` that is not a state‑highway) – the style falls back to this for most county roads |
| `road-shield-5` | **Canadian Provincial** (white‑red) | `CA:AB`, `CA:BC`, … |
| `road-shield-6` | **Canadian National** (black‑white) | `CA:CN` |
| `road-shield-7` | **European (E‑road)** (blue‑white) | `EU:E` |
| `road-shield-8` | **International (A‑road, B‑road, etc.)** | `EU:A`, `EU:B`, `EU:D` |
| `road-shield-9` | **Australian / New‑Zealand** | `AU:NR`, `NZ:SH` |
| `road-shield-10` | **Asian (AH‑road)** | `AS:AH` |
| `road-shield-11` | **Other / generic** (white‑black) | Any network that does not match the above (fallback) |
| `road-shield-12` | **No‑badge (transparent)** – used when the style wants to hide the badge entirely | `none` (the style never actually picks this, but it is kept for completeness) |

> **Note:** The mapping is performed in the style’s `icon-image` expression (see the style source below). If you add a custom network value you want to display, you must add a matching entry to that expression **or** add a sprite with the same name you reference manually.

---

## 2. Get the official sprite sheet (the easiest way)

The OpenMapTiles “streets” style ships with a ready‑made sprite that already contains the 12 shield images, plus all the other icons the style uses (poi symbols, building icons, etc.).

### Hosted version (no build step)

```
https://openmaptiles.org/sprites/streets-v8/sprite.json
https://openmaptiles.org/sprites/streets-v8/sprite.png
```

If you need the high‑DPI version (2× for Retina / high‑resolution displays):

```
https://openmaptiles.org/sprites/streets-v8/sprite@2x.json
https://openmaptiles.org/sprites/streets-v8/sprite@2x.png
```

Just set the `sprite` property of your style (or the `sprite` option you pass to `maplibregl.Map`) to the base URL **without** the file extension:

```js
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'https://openmaptiles.org/styles/streets/style.json',
  // <-- the style already points to the correct sprite, but if you override it:
  // sprite: 'https://openmaptiles.org/sprites/streets-v8/sprite',
  center: [-122.44, 37.76],
  zoom: 12
});
```

That URL will automatically load the `*.json` and `*.png` (or the `@2x` pair if the browser reports a device pixel ratio ≥ 1.5).

### From the GitHub repo (if you want to host it yourself)

1. Clone the repo (or just download the folder)  

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/openmaptiles/openmaptiles.git
   cd openmaptiles/styles/streets
   ```

2. The sprite files live in `sprite/`:

   ```
   sprite/sprite.json
   sprite/sprite.png
   sprite/sprite@2x.json
   sprite/sprite@2x.png
   ```

3. Upload those four files to your static‑file host (e.g. S3, GitHub Pages, Netlify) and point the style’s `sprite` property at the base URL you chose.

---

## 3. If you *must* create or edit a sprite sheet yourself

### a. What you need to include

| File | Must contain |
|------|--------------|
| `sprite.json` | A JSON dictionary where each key is the **exact** sprite name (`road-shield-1`, … `road-shield-12`) and the value is an object with `width`, `height`, `x`, `y`, `pixelRatio`. |
| `sprite.png` | A single PNG that packs all the individual shield PNGs at the coordinates described in `sprite.json`. |
| (optional) `sprite@2x.*` | Same as above but double the pixel dimensions for high‑DPI displays. |

### b. Tools to generate the sprite

| Tool | Quick command |
|------|---------------|
| **SpriteZero** (Node) | `npx @mapbox/spritezero ./icons ./sprite` – put your 12 shield PNGs (named exactly as the keys) in `./icons`. |
| **Mapbox Studio** (web UI) | Upload the 12 PNGs, export the style, and download the generated sprite. |
| **svg2png + ImageMagick** | If you have SVG source files, rasterise them to 64 × 64 (or 128 × 128 for @2x) and then pack with `spritezero`. |

**Important:** The PNGs must be **transparent** PNGs with the badge shape (red‑white‑red, blue‑white, etc.) and **no extra padding**. The default OpenMapTiles shields are 64 × 64 px (32 × 32 px for @2x). If you use a different size you must also edit the style’s `icon-size` expression – but that defeats the “no‑layer‑edit” requirement, so stick with the default dimensions.

### c. Naming the individual PNG files

When you run `spritezero`, the **filename (without extension)** becomes the sprite name. So you need files named exactly:

```
road-shield-1.png
road-shield-2.png
road-shield-3.png
…
road-shield-12.png
```

If you prefer a different naming scheme, you must also edit the style’s `icon-image` expression, which you said you want to avoid.

---

## 4. Verify that the sprite is actually being loaded

Add a temporary layer that draws one of the shield icons directly, bypassing the `icon-image` expression:

```js
map.addLayer({
  id: 'shield-test',
  type: 'symbol',
  source: 'openmaptiles',
  'source-layer': 'transportation',
  filter: ['==', ['get', 'ref'], '95'], // any feature that has a ref
  layout: {
    'icon-image': 'road-shield-1', // force a known sprite
    'icon-size': 1,
    'text-field': ['get', 'ref'],
    'text-font': ['Open Sans Bold'],
    'text-size': 12,
    'text-offset': [0, 0.6]
  },
  paint: {}
});
```

If you see the red‑white‑red Interstate badge behind the “95”, the sprite is correctly loaded. If you still see only the number, open the browser dev‑tools → **Network** tab and look for requests to `sprite.json` / `sprite.png`. A 404 or a CORS error means the URL is wrong or the server isn’t serving the files with the correct MIME type.

---

1. **Make sure your style points at a sprite sheet that contains the 12 shield images.**
